title: Das alte Mütterchen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 208. Text from Wikisource („Das alte Mütterchen (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: An old widow in a great city has outlived her husband, her two children, and every other relative down to her last friend, and sits alone one evening in bitter grief. Hearing the bell for early Mass, she goes to a church lit by no candles but a strange dim light and finds it filled with her dead kin in their old clothes; a kinswoman shows her, at the altar, what became of her two sons in the life they never lived, and tells her God had taken them as innocent children instead. She goes home trembling, thanks God on her knees, and dies three days later.

sentences.t: Es war in einer großen Stadt ein altes Mütterchen, das saß Abends allein in seiner Kammer:
sentences.l: There was in a great city an old little-mother, who sat of an evening alone in her chamber:
sentences.i: In a great city there lived an old little mother, who was sitting one evening alone in her chamber.
sentences.n: “Mütterchen” is the affectionate diminutive of Mutter — a “little old mother,” used tenderly of an old woman (no diminution of respect). The pronoun is neuter throughout (“es/ihm/sein”) because Mütterchen is grammatically neuter — read it as “she/her/her.” “Abends” is the genitive-of-time (“of an evening, in the evenings”), still felt as an idiom in Grimm’s German. The colon at the end sets up the free indirect thought that follows.

sentences.t: es dachte so darüber nach wie es erst den Mann, dann die beiden Kinder, nach und nach alle Verwandte, endlich auch heute noch den letzten Freund verloren hätte und nun ganz allein und verlassen wäre.
sentences.l: she thought over it thus, how she had first lost the husband, then the two children, one by one all relatives, finally even today still the last friend, and was now quite alone and forsaken.
sentences.i: she was thinking over how she had lost first her husband, then her two children, one by one all her relatives, and now this very day the last friend she had — and was now entirely alone and forsaken.
sentences.n: “dachte … nach” is the separable nachdenken — to think through, ponder. The subjunctives “verloren hätte” and “wäre” carry the whole train as reported thought: German uses subjunctive II to mark it as hers, not the narrator’s assertion. “nach und nach” = one by one, little by little. “verlassen” here is the past participle of verlassen (to abandon) used adjectivally — forsaken.

sentences.t: Da ward es in tiefstem Herzen traurig,
sentences.l: Then she became sorrowful in deepest heart,
sentences.i: Then she grew sad to her very heart,
sentences.n: “ward” is the archaic preterite of werden (became); modern German uses “wurde.” “tiefstem Herzen” is the superlative of tief in a dative singular after in — a bare adjective without an article, so the strong ending -em. The phrase is fixed: “in her deepest heart, to her heart’s core.”

sentences.t: und vor allem schwer war ihm der Verlust der beiden Söhne, daß es in seinem Schmerz Gott darüber anklagte.
sentences.l: and above all heavy to her was the loss of the two sons, so that in her pain she reproached God over it.
sentences.i: and above all, the loss of her two sons weighed on her, so that in her grief she reproached God for it.
sentences.n: “ihm” is dative — the burden falls on her: heavy to her. The daß-clause is consecutive — so heavy that. “anklagen” (an + klagen) is here “to accuse, reproach”; “darüber” (dar + über) points back to the loss — for it, over it.

sentences.t: So saß es still und in sich versunken, als es auf einmal zur Frühkirche läuten hörte.
sentences.l: So she sat still and sunk into herself, when all at once she heard the ringing for the early-church.
sentences.i: So she sat still, sunk in herself, when all at once she heard the bell ringing for the early service.
sentences.n: “in sich versunken” = sunken into oneself, lost in one’s own thoughts. “Frühkirche” is the early Mass, the first church service of the morning — the pre-dawn service that opens the tale’s vision. “läuten hörte” is an accusative-with-infinitive: hearing the [bell] ring, though only the infinitive appears.

sentences.t: Es wunderte sich daß es die ganze Nacht also in Leid durchwacht hätte, zündete seine Leuchte an und gieng zur Kirche.
sentences.l: She marvelled that she had thus watched through the whole night in sorrow, kindled her lamp and went to the church.
sentences.i: She marvelled that she had watched through the whole night in sorrow like this; she lit her lamp and went to the church.
sentences.n: “durchwacht” is the perfective of durchwachen — to keep watch through, to stay up through (the night). The subjunctive “hätte” is reported thought again. “zündete … an” is separable anzünden (to light, to kindle). “Leuchte” is a light, a lamp — a broad old word for whatever gives light. “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of ging (went).

sentences.t: Bei seiner Ankunft war sie schon erhellt, aber nicht, wie gewöhnlich, von Kerzen, sondern von einem dämmernden Licht.
sentences.l: On her arrival it was already lit, but not, as usual, by candles, but by a dim light.
sentences.i: On her arrival it was already lit up, not, as usual, by candles, but by a dim, twilit light.
sentences.n: “seiner” is the possessive of the neuter Mütterchen (grammatically its arrival = her arrival); “sie” is die Kirche (feminine). “erhellt” is the past participle of erhellen — to light up, illuminate. “dämmernden” is the present participle of dämmern (to grow dim, to glimmer at twilight) — a half-light glow, not full brightness.

sentences.t: Sie war auch schon angefüllt mit Menschen, und alle Plätze waren besetzt,
sentences.l: It was already filled up with people, and all the seats were taken,
sentences.n: “Sie” is still the church. “angefüllt” is the past participle of anfüllen — to fill up (separable an-). “Plätze” here are the seats or places in the pews.

sentences.t: und als das Mütterchen zu seinem gewöhnlichen Sitz kam, war er auch nicht mehr ledig, sondern die ganze Bank gedrängt voll.
sentences.l: and when the little-mother came to her usual seat, it too was no longer empty, but the whole bench crowded full.
sentences.i: and when the little mother came to her usual seat, that too was no longer free, but the whole bench crowded full.
sentences.n: “ledig” has the old sense “empty, unoccupied” (of a seat) — not the modern “unmarried.” “er” refers to der Sitz (masc.). “gedrängt voll” = pressed full, packed close; “die ganze Bank [war] gedrängt voll” elides the verb, carried over from the previous clause.

sentences.t: Und wie es die Leute ansah, so waren es lauter verstorbene Verwandten, die saßen da in ihren altmodischen Kleidern aber mit blassem Angesicht.
sentences.l: And as she looked at the people, they were nothing but dead relatives, who sat there in their old-fashioned clothes but with pale face.
sentences.i: And as she looked at the people, they were nothing but dead relatives, sitting there in their old-fashioned clothes but with pale faces.
sentences.n: “wie … ansah” = as she looked at (ansehen, separable an-). “lauter” before a plural means “nothing but, only” — pure, unmixed. “verstorbene” is the past participle of versterben, the polite German word for having died. “altmodischen” = old-fashioned; the clothes belong to the ages these relatives died in. “blassem Angesicht” is a fixed singular for all of them together — collectively they wear a pallor.

sentences.t: Sie sprachen auch nicht und sangen nicht,
sentences.l: They did not speak either, and did not sing,
sentences.n: “auch nicht … und … nicht” pairs like English “neither … nor.” The silence is deliberate — no voices in this congregation, only what follows.

sentences.t: es gieng aber ein leises Summen und Wehen durch die Kirche.
sentences.l: there went, however, a soft humming and rustling through the church.
sentences.i: but a soft humming and rustling was passing through the church.
sentences.n: “es gieng … durch” is an impersonal construction — es fills the subject slot while the real subject (“ein leises Summen und Wehen”) is postponed for weight. “Wehen” is the noun of wehen (to blow, to breathe) — a light stir, a breath of sound. “leises” = soft, quiet.

sentences.t: Da stand eine Muhme auf, trat vor, und sprach zu dem Mütterlein „dort sieh nach dem Altar, da wirst du deine Söhne sehen.“
sentences.l: Then a kinswoman stood up, stepped forward, and spoke to the little-mother “look yonder toward the altar, there you will see your sons.”
sentences.i: Then a Muhme stood up, stepped forward, and said to the little mother, “look yonder toward the altar; there you will see your sons.”
sentences.n: “Muhme” is an older German kinship word — an aunt or an older female cousin (broadly, a kinswoman). Grimm keeps the word where a modern telling would say “Tante.” “Mütterlein” is a second diminutive of Mutter, alongside Mütterchen, sometimes used interchangeably. “stand … auf” is separable aufstehen (to stand up); “trat vor” is vortreten (to step forward). Read “du/dein” throughout as English “you/your.”

sentences.t: Die Alte blickte hin und sah ihre beiden Kinder, der eine hieng am Galgen, der andere war auf das Rad geflochten.
sentences.l: The old woman looked over and saw her two children, the one hung on the gallows, the other was woven onto the wheel.
sentences.i: The old woman looked and saw her two children — one hung on the gallows, the other broken on the wheel.
sentences.n: “blickte hin” = looked over (separable hin-, motion away from the speaker). “hieng” is the 1857 spelling of hing (past of hängen, to hang). “auf das Rad geflochten” — literally “woven, braided onto the wheel”: the medieval execution of breaking on the wheel and lashing the body to it. Grimm reports it plainly.

sentences.t: Da sprach die Muhme „siehst du, so wär es ihnen ergangen, wären sie im Leben geblieben und hätte sie Gott nicht als unschuldige Kinder zu sich genommen.“
sentences.l: Then the Muhme spoke, “you see, thus would it have gone for them, had they remained in life and had God not taken them to himself as innocent children.”
sentences.i: Then the Muhme said, “you see, that is how it would have gone with them, had they stayed alive and had God not taken them to himself as innocent children.”
sentences.n: The whole speech is in the counter-factual subjunctive II — “wär … ergangen … wären … geblieben … hätte … genommen” — describing an alternative life that did not happen. “es ergeht einem” is the impersonal idiom “to fare, to go for someone.” “zu sich nehmen” = to take to oneself — to take up into heaven. Read “du/dich” as English “you.”

sentences.t: Die Alte gieng zitternd nach Haus und dankte Gott auf den Knieen daß er es besser mit ihr gemacht hätte als sie hätte begreifen können;
sentences.l: The old woman went trembling home and thanked God on her knees that he had done better with her than she could have grasped;
sentences.i: The old woman went home trembling and thanked God on her knees that he had done better by her than she could have understood;
sentences.n: “auf den Knieen” = on her knees (dative plural of Knie); the 1857 -ien spelling of the modern Knien. “hätte … können” is reported subjunctive again — her own thought carried in her thanks. “begreifen” = to grasp, understand (mentally take hold of).

sentences.t: und am dritten Tag legte sie sich und starb.
sentences.l: and on the third day she lay down and died.
sentences.n: “legte sich” is reflexive — she laid herself down (for the last time). The plainness holds to the end; the tale does not sermonise.

glossary.besetzt: besetzt — occupied, taken (past part. of besetzen used adjectivally; of seats)
glossary.gedrängt: drängen — to press, crowd (past participle used adverbially; gedrängt voll = crowded full)
glossary.ledig: ledig — empty, unoccupied (older sense, of a seat; not the modern “unmarried” or “rid of”)
glossary.rad: das Rad — wheel; here the medieval execution-wheel on which a body was broken
glossary.sitz: der Sitz — seat, place (masc. noun; here of the little mother’s usual place on the church bench)
